newsitem.title: CZECH REPUBLIC: Czechs should let crown depreciate - economist.
newsitem.headline: Czechs should let crown depreciate - economist.

text.p: The Czech central bank should allow the crown to depreciate to help exports and should not intervene even if it falls to the low end of its fluctuation band, Jan Svejnar, director of the Economics Institute at the Czech Academy of Sciences told Reuters on Thursday.
In an interview, Svejnar said without central bank intervention, the market could push the crown as low as 20 percent below parity with its mark/dollar basket.

Contrary to published reports in local media, Svejnar said he was not advising a direct administrative devaluation of the currency, but rather for the bank to allow a market-driven depreciation to pull it down as it naturally would under the existing macroecnomic situation.

"I'm not saying that the central bank should go and devalue. I'm saying that it should be ready to let the currency depreciate if and when the investors move the rate," Svejnar, who is also a professor of economics and the University of Michigan, told Reuters.
"I don't think they have to intervene at all. I think there is a very strong equilibrating mechanism. I wouldn't be surprised if it went down to a 20 percent differential for instance."

The crown, facing a current account deficit which has exceeded eight percent of gross domestic product, last week fell to a nine-month low against the basket after record levels of 5.51 percent above parity in early February.

The central bank, since widening its corridor in February 1996 from plus/minus 0.5 percent, has virtually matched the market each day in its fixing. On Thursday, the crown firmed to +1.39 percent, after a deviation of +1.26 on Thursday.
The central bank and the government, meanwhile, have repeatedly ruled out a direct devaluation of the crown to boost exports.

"What I am more worried about is... sooner or later (the trade balance) will become untenable in the sense that the western capital investors who have caused a significant inflow of capital here...will start pulling their resources out," Svejnar said.
He said that with the central bank holding foreign exchange reserves covering just about five months of average imports, central bank intervention to prop up the crown would be futile.
Svejnar said that Czechs "should take a lesson" from the 1992 crash of the British pound when the Bank of England made a fruitless attempt to defend its currency against speculators.

"Imagine if you lost (reserves) overnight because you are trying to intervene, then you're going to have to let the currency depreciate anyway because you no longer have reserves, and you have no cushion to work with in case there is some external shocks," Svejnar said.
